source_refs.note: Topic 3.3 with Figs. 3.11 to 3.14, Example 3.4 and the side boxes (PDF 62-65, printed 59-62). Numerical 3.7's printed answer unit (km h^-1) is unclear in the source; recorded as a finding.

blocks.text: Satellites are objects that orbit in a nearly circular path around the Earth; they are put into orbit by rockets and held in orbit by the gravitational pull of the Earth. Low-flying Earth satellites have acceleration 9.8 m s^-2 towards the centre of the Earth; if there were no gravitational pull they would fly off in a straight line along the tangent to the orbit. A satellite moving in a circle has an acceleration v^2/r, and in a circular orbit around the Earth the centripetal acceleration is supplied by gravity: g = v^2 / R ... (3.14), where v is the orbital velocity and R the radius of the Earth (6400 km). From Eq. 3.14, v = sqrt(gR) = sqrt(9.8 m s^-2 x 6.4 x 10^6 m) = 7.9 x 10^3 m s^-1 = 7.9 km s^-1.

blocks.title: Critical velocity and period
blocks.text: 7.9 km s^-1 is the minimum velocity necessary to put a satellite into orbit, called the critical velocity. The period T is T = 2 pi R / v = 2 x 3.14 x 6400 km / 7.9 km s^-1 = 5060 s = 84 min approximately.

If, however, a satellite in a circular orbit is at a distance h much greater than R above the Earth's surface, we must take into account the experimental fact that the gravitational acceleration decreases inversely as the square of the distance from the centre of the Earth (Fig. 3.11). The higher the satellite, the slower the required speed and the longer it takes to complete one revolution around the Earth. The satellite-orbits box shows the escape speed of 11 km s^-1 (40 000 km h^-1), a circular orbit at 27 000 km h^-1 and an elliptical orbit at 30 000 km h^-1. Newton predicted artificial satellites about 300 years ago in his Principia Mathematica: if an object is thrown horizontally from a sufficiently high place with a sufficiently high speed, it will start revolving around the Earth (Do you know).

blocks.text: Fig. 3.12 shows a satellite of mass m_s going round the Earth, of mass M, in a circular path of radius r with orbital speed v. A centripetal force m_s v^2 / r is required to hold the satellite in orbit, provided by the gravitational attraction between the Earth and the satellite. Equating the gravitational force to the required centripetal force, G m_s M / r^2 = m_s v^2 / r, or v = sqrt(GM/r) ... (3.15). This shows that the mass of the satellite is unimportant in describing its orbit: any satellite orbiting at distance r from the Earth's centre must have the orbital speed given by Eq. 3.15, and any speed less than this brings the satellite tumbling back to the Earth.

blocks.alt: The Earth at the centre of a circular orbit. A satellite on the orbit is joined to the Earth's centre by a line carrying an arrow F towards the Earth, and an arrow from the satellite points along the tangent to the orbit. Labels: Earth, Satellite, F.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.12: A satellite going round the Earth in a circular orbit (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.12).

blocks.title: Example 3.4
blocks.text: An Earth satellite is in circular orbit at a distance of 384 000 km from the Earth's surface. What is its period of one revolution in days? Take M = 6.0 x 10^24 kg and R = 6400 km. Solution: r = R + h = (6400 + 384 000) km = 390 400 km. Using v = sqrt(GM/r) = sqrt(6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2 x 6 x 10^24 kg / 390 400 km) = 1.025 km s^-1. Also T = 2 pi r / v = 2 x 3.14 x 390 400 km x (1/1.025 km s^-1) x (1 day / (60 x 60 x 24 s)) = 27.7 days.

When a satellite is launched by a rocket into its desired orbit around the Earth, everything inside it experiences weightlessness, because the satellite is accelerating towards the centre of the Earth as a freely falling body. Consider a satellite of mass M revolving in its orbit of radius r around the Earth, and a body of mass m inside it suspended by a spring balance from the ceiling (Fig. 3.13). Two forces act on the body: its weight mg downward, and the supporting force, the normal force F_N or tension in the spring, upward. Their resultant equals the centripetal force required by the mass m, acting towards the centre of the Earth: Fc = mg - F_N ... (3.16), where Fc = m v^2 / r, hence m v^2 / r = mg - F_N ... (3.16-a). The centripetal force responsible for the revolution of the satellite is provided by the gravitational attraction between the Earth and the satellite: F_g = Fc, Mg = M v^2 / r, so g = v^2 / r. Hence Eq. 3.16-a becomes mg = mg - F_N, or F_N = 0. The supporting force acting on a body inside the satellite is zero, so the bodies and the astronauts in a satellite find themselves in a state of apparent weightlessness. Your weight changes slightly only when the velocity of a lift changes, at the start and end of a ride, not while the velocity is constant (Do You Know); when a bucket full of water is whirled rapidly in a vertical circle the water does not fall out even when the bucket is inverted at the top (Can you tell). In 1984, at a height of 100 km above Hawaii and a speed of 29 000 km h^-1, Bruce McCandless stepped into space from a space shuttle and became the first human satellite of the Earth (Tid-bits).

blocks.text: In gravity-free space no force pushes anybody to any side of the spacecraft. If the spacecraft is to stay in orbit for an extended period, the weightlessness may affect the performance of the astronauts; to overcome this an artificial gravity can be created so that the crew can function almost normally. The spaceship is set into rotation about its own axis; the astronaut is then pressed towards the outer rim and exerts a force on the floor of the spaceship much as on the Earth. Consider a spacecraft of the shape in Fig. 3.14: its outer radius is R and it rotates about its central axis with angular speed omega, so its centripetal acceleration is a_c = R omega^2. But omega = 2 pi / T, where T is the period of revolution of the spaceship, hence a_c = R (2 pi)^2 / T^2 = R 4 pi^2 / T^2. As the frequency f = 1/T, a_c = R 4 pi^2 f^2, or f^2 = a_c / (4 pi^2 R), or f = (1/(2 pi)) sqrt(a_c / R). As described above, the force of gravity provides the required centripetal acceleration, so a_c = g and f = (1/(2 pi)) sqrt(g / R) ... (3.17). When the spaceship rotates with this frequency, an artificial gravity like the Earth's is provided to its inhabitants: the surface of the rotating ship pushes on an object in contact with it and so provides the centripetal force that keeps the object moving on a circular path (Do You Know).
